title: IB Revision Active Recall: A Weekly Study Plan
summary: IB revision active recall made practical: follow a weekly study plan using retrieval, spaced review, feedback, and exam-style questions across IB subjects.
body_markdown:
IB revision active recall works when study begins with a question, not an open textbook. For IB Diploma students, the method is simple: retrieve a topic from memory, check the answer, record the gap, and revisit it after an interval. Build those steps into each week and revision becomes a repeatable system.


Six subjects compete with coursework, Theory of Knowledge, and the Extended Essay. Your goal is to identify what you can recall independently and direct your limited time toward what you cannot.


### How IB revision active recall works


Active recall means deliberately producing an answer from memory. That can involve explaining photosynthesis aloud, reconstructing a historical argument, writing a formula, sketching an economic model, or listing quotations before checking the source.


The checking stage is essential. Without it, a confident mistake can become familiar. Birmingham City University's[guide to active recall and spaced repetition](https://www.bcu.ac.uk/exams-and-revision/best-ways-to-revise/active-recall) recommends reviewing material at increasing intervals, with examples such as one day, three days, and one week later.


A practical retrieval loop has four steps:


1. Choose a precise prompt.
2. Answer with all resources closed.
3. Compare your response with reliable notes or a mark scheme.
4. Schedule another attempt based on the result.


If the answer was complete, lengthen the interval. If it was partial, revisit it sooner. For more detail, see RevisionDojo's guide to[spaced repetition for IB revision](https://www.revisiondojo.com/blog/spaced-repetition-ib-revision) .


A student asks a talking textbook to stay quiet during a recall attempt


### Your weekly study plan at a glance


Day Active recall task Useful evidence


Monday Write everything remembered about one recent topic Missing concepts


Tuesday Convert gaps into flashcards or short questions Accuracy after feedback


Wednesday Answer 2-4 exam-style questions Mark scheme omissions


Thursday Retrieve weak material again Improvement since Monday


Friday Mix old and new topics Ability to choose the right method


Weekend Complete one timed response Timing, structure, and precision


The important shift is from measuring time to measuring evidence. Two hours of rereading can feel smooth while revealing little. One closed-book response shows exactly where understanding breaks down.


RevisionDojo makes that evidence easier to collect. Use **Study Notes** to check accuracy, **Flashcards** for short prompts, and the **Questionbank** to move from factual recall into application. The[best way to revise for IB exams](https://www.revisiondojo.com/blog/what-s-the-best-way-to-revise-for-ib-exams) follows a similar loop of planning, retrieval, practice, and error review.


### Balance recall across IB subjects


Not every subject should use identical prompts. In Biology, retrieve processes and then apply them to unfamiliar data. In Mathematics, recall the method before solving a problem without worked steps. In English, retrieve textual evidence, then explain how it supports an interpretation. In History, reconstruct a line of argument rather than memorising isolated dates.


This is why flashcards are useful but insufficient on their own. They test compact knowledge well, while extended responses test selection, structure, and judgement. RevisionDojo's[science of spaced repetition](https://www.revisiondojo.com/blog/the-science-of-spaced-repetition-for-ap-ib-success) explains how retrieval and spacing can work together rather than as separate techniques.


### Build feedback into the plan


A weekly plan improves only if mistakes influence the next week. Keep a short error log with three labels:


- **Knowledge gap:** the fact, quotation, or formula was missing
- **Application gap:** the knowledge was available but used incorrectly
- **Communication gap:** the answer lacked structure, terminology, or sufficient explanation


RevisionDojo's **AI Chat** can help clarify a confusing concept, while **Grading tools** can provide another feedback point for written answers. **Predicted Papers** and **Mock Exams** support timed practice when exams approach. For longer assignments, the **Coursework Library** and **Tutors** can help students understand expectations and act on feedback without replacing independent work.


Students who need a broader planning framework can also use RevisionDojo's guide to[time management tools for IB students](https://www.revisiondojo.com/blog/best-time-management-tools-for-ib-students) .


### Make the plan sustainable


Leave space for deadlines, fatigue, and topics that take longer than expected. Each weekend, choose priorities based on retrieval results.


Active recall makes uncertainty visible. RevisionDojo brings practice, resources, and feedback together as a complete IB resource, helping you turn those gaps into purposeful revision.
